# Block 6: Build your own agent in R {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(webexercises)
```

In this block you build the two parts of an agent yourself: a conversation and
a tool. Then you run a complete agent on a real task and approve every step it
takes. The task is a common one: translate a short piece of old base R code
into tidyverse code, and prove that the translation gives the same answer.
After this, every control from Blocks 3 to 5 is something you can see in code.

*⏱ ~35 minutes · Start on `main`, Git pane clean, with your API key saved as
`AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY` ([setup](11a-setup-claude-code.qmd#api-key)). Claude
Code is not used in this block.*

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
## This block's files, and how it fits

You stay in your workshop repository, on `main`, straight after lunch. Claude
Code is set aside: you use an agent that you can read line by line. You give it
the translation task that the shipped `tests/test_translation.R` checks.
Nothing later in the day uses its output. So if time is short, your instructor
may run Task 2 on screen while you decide each approval in the chat.

| File | Where it comes from | Its job here |
|---|---|---|
| `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv` | Shipped; used since Block 2 | The data the translation summarises |
| `scripts/functions/load_voles.R` | Shipped; used since Block 3 | Reads the data with fixed column types |
| `agent/mini_agent.R` | Shipped; first used here | The agent: three tools, its own permission rule and Manual-mode approvals |
| `tests/test_translation.R` | Shipped; first used here | Holds the original base R code, `legacy_rate_summary()`, and compares the translation with it |
| `scripts/functions/summaries.R` | Written by your agent, with your approval, in Task 2 | The translation |
| A line in `docs/ai-log.md` | You, in Task 2 | The record |

**Before you start.** ellmer is the package that talks to Claude and runs the
loop. It is pinned in your repository's `renv.lock`, so `renv::restore()`
installed it. Never run `install.packages()` inside the project. Your key
comes from an Anthropic Console account, which is separate from a Claude
subscription. The key lives in your user-level `.Renviron`, outside every
repository. Every request costs a little; Task 2 shows you how much the agent
used.

The page follows the order of Hadley Wickham's explainer
[*What is an agent?*](https://substack.hadley.nz/p/what-is-an-agent): a
conversation, then a tool, then the loop. Joseph Barbier's talk *50 lines of
code to rebuild Claude Code in R* (R+AI 2026, scheduled for 10 November) shows
how to build the same kind of agent; the version here is our own.
:::


## Task 1: a conversation, then a tool

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Talk to a model, then give it a tool (8 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** see what one request to a model is, what a model cannot do on its
own, and what a tool request is, so that nothing your agent does in Task 2 is
a surprise.

**1. Have a conversation.** Run this in the R console:

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(ellmer)

key <- function() Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY")
chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$chat("Tell me a joke about R.")
chat$chat("Explain why it is funny, in one sentence.")
chat$chat("How many days is it until 25 December?")
chat
```

Printing `chat` shows the conversation as `r glossary("turn", "turns")`. The
second question works only because ellmer sends the **whole conversation so
far** with each request: the model keeps nothing between requests ("the LLM
API is stateless", in Wickham's words). That is the
[context window](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd) from Block 1. It is also why
a long conversation costs more per question.

The memory is the `chat` object in your R session. It lasts as long as that
object does, and nothing is saved to disk. Restart R, or create a new `chat`
(as step 2 does), and the conversation starts again from nothing.

Now read the third answer. A model on its own only produces text. It has no
clock, and it cannot run code, open your files or change them. Today's date is
"a question that cannot be part of its training data" (Wickham), so the model
can only say it does not know, ask you, or guess, and a guess reads as
confidently as a fact. The same holds for anything it tells you about data or
code it has not been shown: it predicts; it does not check.

**2. Give it a tool.** A `r glossary("tools", "tool")` "is just a different
name for a function, but importantly it's a function that's run on your
computer" (Wickham). Tools let a model get data about the world as it is
today, and take actions:

```{r}
#| eval: false
today <- tool(
  function() format(Sys.Date()),
  name = "today",
  description = "Get today's date."
)

chat <- chat_anthropic(model = "claude-sonnet-5-5", credentials = key)
chat$register_tool(today)
chat$chat("How many days is it until 25 December?")
chat
```

The model sees only the tool's name, description and arguments (here, none),
so the description is all it has to decide when the tool is useful. Its first
reply is a request: "call `today`". ellmer runs `today()` **on your computer**
and sends the result back. Then the model answers, now from a fact rather
than a guess. That is two `r glossary("request", "requests")` for one
question. This new `chat` knows nothing of the joke: it is a new conversation.

**You are done when** you can point, in the printed `chat`, to the tool
request and to the tool result, say which of them ran on your computer, and
say why the same question in step 1 could not get a reliable answer.

**If it goes wrong:** if the first `chat$chat()` reports a missing or invalid
key, check `Sys.getenv("AGENT_ANTHROPIC_KEY") != ""`. Restart R after you edit
`.Renviron`.

::::
:::


## The loop

An `r glossary("agent")` repeats that exchange until a reply asks for no tool.
Wickham's definition: "An agent is an LLM, in a harness, that calls tools
repeatedly in a loop, deciding each next step from the last result." Each
time, the `r glossary("harness")` sends the conversation, runs any tool the
model asks for, adds the result, and sends it all again. Every control in this
course acts on one of three facts:

- **The model only asks.** The harness runs each tool on your computer, so
  that is where Manual mode asks you, a deny rule refuses, and a hook inspects.
- **Results go back to the model.** A tool that reads a data file sends that
  data to the provider:
  [Block 3's disclosure route](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd).
- **The model decides when to stop.** It can loop longer than you expect.
  That is why a real harness has limits on how long it may run, and a
  **stop key** that interrupts it mid-loop: Esc in Claude Code
  ([Block 1](11-AI-programming-integrated.qmd)). In R, you interrupt
  `chat$chat()` as you would any long-running code: Esc in the RStudio
  console, or `Ctrl+C` in a terminal. Your mini agent sets no limit of its
  own; your approvals are its brake.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## How it works: the loop with no model at all

This code runs without an API key. It replaces the model with a pretend one
that follows a script. Each pass of `repeat` is one request.

```{r}
# the tools, as plain R functions
tools <- list(
  n_rows = function(name) {
    nrow(get(name, envir = as.environment("package:datasets")))
  }
)

# a pretend model: asks for a tool until it has two results, then answers
pretend_model <- function(turns) {
  results <- Filter(function(t) t$role == "tool result", turns)
  if (length(results) == 0) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "mtcars"))
  } else if (length(results) == 1) {
    list(role = "assistant", tool = "n_rows", args = list(name = "iris"))
  } else {
    list(role = "assistant",
         text = paste("iris has", results[[2]]$text, "rows and mtcars has",
                      results[[1]]$text, "so iris has more."))
  }
}

# the harness: send the conversation, run any tool asked for, repeat
question <- "Which has more rows, mtcars or iris?"
turns <- list(list(role = "user", text = question))
repeat {
  reply <- pretend_model(turns)
  turns <- c(turns, list(reply))
  if (is.null(reply$tool)) break # no tool asked for: this is the answer
  result <- do.call(tools[[reply$tool]], reply$args)
  turns <- c(turns, list(list(role = "tool result", text = result)))
}

for (t in turns) {
  what <- if (is.null(t$tool)) t$text else
    paste0("call ", t$tool, "(", t$args, ")")
  cat(sprintf("%-12s %s\n", t$role, what))
}
```

`do.call()` is the only line that does anything to your computer: that is
where Manual mode, deny rules and hooks act. In the real API the tool result
goes back inside a user turn; ellmer does that for you.
:::


## Your agent: `agent/mini_agent.R`

Your repository ships a complete agent of about 80 lines, built from the same
parts. It has one job: translate a short base R function into tidyverse code,
run a test that compares the two, and fix its code until they match. Your
instructor walks through it. Each part matches something from this morning.

**Three tools.** Each is an R function, described to the model by a name, a
description and its arguments:

| Tool | The model sends | What runs on your computer | What goes back to the model | Asks you first? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `read_file()` | a path | `readLines()` on that file, if `allowed()` agrees | the file's text | No |
| `write_file()` | a path under `scripts/`, and the whole new file | `writeLines()`, if `allowed()` agrees | "Wrote …" | Yes |
| `run_test()` | nothing | the shipped test `tests/test_translation.R`, in a `r glossary("fresh R session")` | the last 40 lines of the test's report | Yes |

`run_test()` is how the agent finds out whether its code works. It takes no
arguments, so the model cannot choose another test or hand it code. The test
does three things:

1. runs the original base R function, `legacy_rate_summary()`, which is
   defined inside the test file;
2. in a second fresh R session, sources `scripts/functions/load_voles.R` and
   the agent's `scripts/functions/summaries.R`, then runs
   `summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles())`;
3. compares the two results once types and row order are normalised: an
   `r glossary("equivalence check")`.

If they match, the report says the test passed. If not, it lists the values
that differ, and the agent reads that list to choose its next fix.

**`allowed()` is its deny rule.** Each path is first made absolute and tidied
(`scripts/../tests` becomes `tests`), then checked. The agent may read anything
inside the project except files named `.Renviron` or `.env`. It may write
**only under `scripts/`**, so it cannot edit its checks in `tests/` or its own
rules in `agent/`.

**`ask_first()` is Manual mode.** Reads go straight through. Every write and
every test run is shown to you first, and is refused unless you choose
**Yes**.

**The `r glossary("system prompt")` is its instruction file.** The agent is
not given your `AGENTS.md`, though it could still open the file, like any
other. Like `AGENTS.md`, its prompt is only a request.

**Predict: which of these does `allowed()` refuse?** Decide before your
instructor runs them.

1. `read_file("data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv")` `r mcq(c("refused", answer = "allowed"))`
2. `read_file("../.Renviron")` `r mcq(c(answer = "refused", "allowed"))`
3. `write_file("scripts/../tests/test_translation.R", …)` `r mcq(c(answer = "refused", "allowed"))`
4. `write_file("scripts/functions/load_voles.R", …)` `r mcq(c("refused", answer = "allowed"))`
5. `read_file(".renviron")`, on Windows or a Mac `r mcq(c("refused", answer = "allowed"))`

`r hide("Why?")`

1. The raw data are inside the project, so the agent may read them, and what
   it reads goes to the provider: Block 3's disclosure route.
2. `../` leaves the project. Your key is in your user-level `.Renviron`,
   outside every project, so it is refused on both counts.
3. The path is tidied before it is checked, so the `..` trick ends in `tests/`.
4. `load_voles.R` is under `scripts/`, so the agent may rewrite it, yet the
   test relies on it: a changed loader could let a wrong translation pass.
   That is one reason to check, at the end, that the Git pane shows only
   `summaries.R`.
5. The check compares names exactly, but Windows and macOS ignore case in file
   names, so `.renviron` opens a project's `.Renviron`, if it has one. A list
   of names covers the names you thought of, like a deny rule in Block 5: it
   prevents, on the routes it names.

`r unhide()`

**The gap is still there.** `run_test()` cannot be handed code, but the test
it runs sources `summaries.R`, and the agent writes that file. Whatever the
agent puts there runs when you choose **Yes** to `run_test()`: a line that
overwrites `data/raw/voles_metabolism.csv`, or one that reads your key with
`Sys.getenv()` and puts it in an error message, which goes back to the model
in the test's report. The model has no reason to do either, but nothing in the
code stops it. `allowed()` decides where the agent's code is saved, not what
that code does when it runs. That is the gap Block 5 found: R code can write
anywhere, whatever the deny rules say. What stands in the way is you, reading
the code at the `write_file` approval before you let the test run it.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Reference: the full `agent/mini_agent.R`

```{r, eval = FALSE, file = here::here("_instructor", "template-files", "agent", "mini_agent.R")}
```

An error in a tool does not stop the agent. ellmer sends the error message back
to the model, which can try something else. So a refused write comes back as
"Refused: …". `run_test()` starts a fresh R session with `callr::r()`, and the
test starts a second one for the agent's code. Fresh sessions keep objects and
loaded packages apart in both directions: nothing the test or the agent's code
loads reaches your session, and nothing loaded in yours can make the test
pass. They do not protect files: code in a fresh session can still write
anywhere. Only the last 40 lines of the test's report go back to the model.
:::


## Task 2: run your agent

:::{.task}
::::{.task-header}
Run your agent (15 minutes)
::::
::::{.task-container}

**Goal:** watch your own agent write, test and fix a translation while you
approve every write and test run, so that you see exactly where Manual mode
and a deny rule act, and what a passing test does and does not tell you.

**Start state:** `main`, Git pane clean, R's working directory at the
repository's root (as it is when you open the project).

**1. Load the agent.** Nothing is sent to the model yet:

```{r}
#| eval: false
source(here::here("agent", "mini_agent.R"))
```

**2. Give it the task.** You ask for a tidyverse version of
`legacy_rate_summary()`, the original base R code. It is in
`tests/test_translation.R`, next to the check that compares the two:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat$chat(paste(
  "Write a function summarise_rate_tidy(data) in scripts/functions/summaries.R",
  "whose output matches legacy_rate_summary() in tests/test_translation.R.",
  "Use dplyr and the native pipe; it must work in a fresh R session.",
  "Write only that file, and no tests. Then run the test with run_test,",
  "and fix the function until it passes."
))
```

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## The original code, and what you are asking for

```{r}
#| eval: false
legacy_rate_summary <- function() {
  voles <- read.csv(
    here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv"),
    stringsAsFactors = TRUE
  )
  rate_mean <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                         data = voles, FUN = mean)
  rate_n <- aggregate(metabolic_rate_post ~ treatment_arm + sex,
                      data = voles, FUN = length)
  names(rate_n)[3] <- "n"
  merge(rate_mean, rate_n, by = c("treatment_arm", "sex"))
}
```

It gives one row for each treatment arm and sex, with the mean metabolic rate
(in a column still called `metabolic_rate_post`) and `n`, the number of
animals. It makes two summaries and then joins them, which is typical of older
base R; `group_by()` and `summarise()` do it in one step.

The test sets one difference: it calls `summarise_rate_tidy(load_voles())`,
so the new function is handed the data instead of reading the file itself.
Everything else must come out the same.

**Predict before you run it:** one animal has no `metabolic_rate_post`. What
does the original do with that animal, and what would a straight
`group_by()` and `summarise()` do? Step 6 checks your answer.
:::

**3. Decide each request.** Reads run without asking. For a `write_file`
request, read the code it prints: it is the code that `run_test()` will run.
Choose **Yes** only for a write to `scripts/functions/summaries.R`.
**Refuse the first `run_test` on purpose,** to see a refusal from the model's
side. ellmer sends back "Tool call rejected. The user has chosen to disallow
the tool call.", and the model decides what to do next. It usually stops and
explains. If it asks again at once, answer No again. Then let it continue:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat$chat("Go ahead and run the test.")
```

**4. Look inside.** Do this before step 5, because restarting R clears `chat`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
chat               # every turn: your prompt, its tool requests, the results
chat$get_tokens()  # the tokens it sent and received, one row per request
```

Find your refusal, any test report that failed, and the write that followed
it. Note how many requests the task took (count the assistant turns) and how
many tokens.

**5. Check its work yourself.** When the agent says "the test passes", that is
a `r glossary("claimed execution", "claim")`. Read the diff of
`scripts/functions/summaries.R` in the Git pane. Then restart R
(*Session → Restart R*) and run:

```{r}
#| eval: false
testthat::test_dir(here::here("tests"))
```

`test_translation.R` is the test that matters here: it now passes rather than
skips. The other files pass or skip, as before.

**6. Check what happened to the missing value.** Find, in the diff, how the
translation handles the animal with no `metabolic_rate_post`, and whether the
agent's last reply mentioned it. Then compare with your prediction.

`r hide("What should happen to the missing value, and why")`

**What the original does.** `aggregate()` with a formula drops every row with a
missing value in the formula's variables (its default is
`na.action = na.omit`), and it says nothing. So the original's mean and `n`
for that animal's group leave the animal out.

**What we expect from the agent.** A straight translation,
`group_by(treatment_arm, sex)` and then
`summarise(metabolic_rate_post = mean(metabolic_rate_post), n = n())`, keeps
the animal: that group gets an `NA` mean and an `n` one too high. The test
fails, and its report shows exactly those two differences. A passing
translation must leave the animal out too, for example with
`filter(!is.na(metabolic_rate_post))` before summarising. So the agent may
notice the missing value only because the test failed, not because it read
the original closely.

**Why it matters.** The test checks "the same as the original", not
"correct". Whether to leave out an animal with a missing measurement is a
scientific decision. The original made it silently, and a passing translation
copies it, silently unless the agent tells you. If it did not, a passing test
has hidden a decision from you; say so in your log line in step 7. Block 8
returns to the difference between "unchanged" and "right".

`r unhide()`

**7. Record and commit.** Your agent can write only under `scripts/`, so it
cannot draft this line as Claude Code did in Block 3: that is its write rule
at work. Add the line to `docs/ai-log.md` yourself, with today's date, for
example
`2026-10-22; mini agent (ellmer, claude-sonnet-5-5); translated the rate summary to tidyverse; kept after reading the diff and running the tests, noting that it drops the animal with a missing rate, as the original does`.
Then commit `summaries.R` and the log.

**You are done when** `test_translation.R` passes in your own run, the Git
pane showed only `summaries.R` and your log changed (not `load_voles.R`, which
the test also relies on), you can say how many requests and tokens the task
took and what happened to the animal with the missing value, and both files
are committed.

**If it goes wrong:**

- **The agent loops or goes off course:** answer **No** at its next request,
  or press Esc to interrupt it. ellmer keeps the conversation, so you can then
  steer it with `chat$chat("…")`, or `source()` the file again to start a new
  conversation.
- **A refused write:** the agent can write only under `scripts/`; read the
  path it asked for.
- **`run_test` cannot find `tests/test_translation.R`:** check that `getwd()`
  is the repository's root.
- **An unwanted change:** **Revert** it in the Git pane.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## What did it cost?

`chat$get_cost()` turns the tokens into money when ellmer knows the model's
price. If it shows `NA`, run `ellmer::models_update_prices()` once to refresh
ellmer's price list. Or multiply the tokens from `chat$get_tokens()` by the
prices on Anthropic's pricing page. `claude-opus-5-5`, named in the comment at
the top of `mini_agent.R`, is a larger model at a higher price per token; to
use it, change the `model` line.
:::

::::
:::


## What Claude Code adds

| Your mini agent | Claude Code |
|---|---|
| `ask_first()` and `tool_reject()` | Manual mode (`default`) and the other permission modes |
| `allowed()`: writes only under `scripts/` | Deny rules in `.claude/settings.json`, such as `Edit(/data/raw/**)` |
| The system prompt | `AGENTS.md`, read at the start of each session |
| `run_test()`, which runs one test, and with it whatever code the agent wrote into `summaries.R` | Any command it asks to run, each with your approval |
| Esc, to interrupt `chat$chat()`; no limit of its own | Esc, to interrupt it mid-task |
| `chat` and `chat$get_tokens()`, kept until you restart R | The conversation itself, and the model shown in Claude Code |
| Git, to see and undo changes | Git, plus `/rewind`, which undoes only changes made with its edit tools ([Block 5](11f-enforced-controls.qmd)) |

Claude Code adds plan mode, hooks, skills, compaction of long conversations,
many more tools and far more checks around each one. You build the small
version to understand the big one, not to use it for real work. In Block 7 you
hand Claude Code a much bigger job under the same controls.


:::{.callout-note}
## Check · Reproduce · Record

- **You can now:** explain an agent as a model, a harness and tools in a loop,
  and run one in R, **trusted because** you can read every line that touches
  your files, including the code the test runs, and a test you did not write
  decides whether its output matches the original.
- **Check:** every write and every run is shown to you before it happens; the
  Git pane shows what changed; the test runs in a fresh R session.
- **Reproduce:** `run_test()` runs in a fresh R session, so the agent's check
  does not depend on what is loaded in yours.
- **Record:** `chat` holds the full record of what was sent and received, until
  you restart R; your AI-use log records the tool, the model and what you kept.
:::


## Check your understanding

**In an agent built with ellmer, who runs a tool's R function?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The model, on Anthropic's servers",
  answer = "The harness (ellmer), on your computer, after the model asks for it",
  "Nobody: the model predicts what the function would return",
  "RStudio, in a separate window"
))`

**In Task 1, why could the model answer "How many days is it until 25 December?" reliably only once it had the `today` tool?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "The second chat used a larger model",
  answer = "A model only produces text from its training and the conversation, and has no clock; the tool ran Sys.Date() on your computer and sent the date back",
  "The tool gave the model access to the internet",
  "ellmer adds today's date to every request"
))`

**True or false: when an agent's tool reads a file, the file's contents are sent to the model provider.** `r torf(TRUE)`

**True or false: after you restart R, `chat` still holds the conversation from Task 2.** `r torf(FALSE)`

**Your agent can write only under `scripts/`. When you choose Yes to `run_test()`, what can the code in `scripts/functions/summaries.R` change?**

`r longmcq(c(
  "Nothing outside scripts/: allowed() refuses it",
  "Nothing on disk: callr::r() runs it in a fresh R session",
  answer = "Any file R can reach, data/raw/ included: allowed() checks where write_file saves code, not what the saved code does",
  "Only the objects in your own R session"
))`


## Going further (not covered live)

This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if
it is useful to you.

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Narrow the write rule to one file

`write_file()` may rewrite any file under `scripts/`, including
`scripts/functions/load_voles.R`, which the test relies on. Give the tool only
the reach the task needs. In `agent/mini_agent.R`, replace the function inside
`write_file` with this one, and `source()` the file again:

```{r}
#| eval: false
function(path, content) {
  full <- allowed(path, folder = fs::path(root, "scripts"))
  if (full != fs::path(root, "scripts", "functions", "summaries.R")) {
    stop("Refused: ", path)
  }
  writeLines(content, full)
  paste("Wrote", path)
}
```

Then ask the agent to change `load_voles.R`. The write is refused before you
are asked. Update the tool's `description` too, so that the model knows the
new limit instead of finding it by trial.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Add a general `run_r()` tool

Add this tool to `agent/mini_agent.R`. Paste it after `run_test`. Add `run_r`
to the `register_tools()` list, and add `"run_r"` to the names that
`ask_first()` asks about. Then `source()` the file again for a new
conversation. (Redefining
`ask_first()` in the console has no effect: the chat keeps the copy it was
given.)

```{r}
#| eval: false
run_r <- tool(
  function(code) {
    out <- callr::r(function(code) utils::capture.output(
      tryCatch(source(exprs = parse(text = code), print.eval = TRUE),
               error = function(e) cat("Error:", conditionMessage(e), "\n"))
    ), list(code = code))
    paste(utils::head(out, 60), collapse = "\n")
  },
  name = "run_r",
  description = "Run R code in a fresh R session; return its printed output.",
  arguments = list(code = type_string("The R code to run."))
)
```

Now the model can run any code straight from a request: `writeLines()` into
`data/raw/`, or `Sys.getenv()` for your key. With `run_test()`, the same code
first had to be saved in a file under `scripts/`, shown to you at a write
approval and left in the Git pane, and then run by a second approval.
`run_r()` removes those steps: the code runs from the request alone and leaves
no file to review. Only your approval stands in the way, exactly as in
Block 5. A narrow tool such as `run_test()` needs less trust than a general
one, but not none.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## A restricted mode

Change `ask_first()` in `agent/mini_agent.R` so that it asks before every
call, reads included. Then `source()` the file again. You now see every file
the agent wants to read before it is sent to the provider. By default, Claude
Code never asks before reading a project file
([Block 3](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd)). In your own agent, one line
of R changes that, because you wrote its approval step.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Packages that do more

- [btw](https://posit-dev.github.io/btw/) gives ellmer agents ready-made tools
  for R: package documentation, your live session's objects and your project's
  files.
- [mcptools](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcptools/) connects R to the Model
  Context Protocol, so R functions can be tools for other assistants, including
  Claude Code.
:::

:::{.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Another provider

ellmer has a `chat_*()` function for each provider it supports. The tools and
the loop stay the same. Tool calling can be much less reliable with small local
models, so start with a hosted model.
:::
